one_liner: Meta's C++ IETF QUIC transport (client+server) under Proxygen HTTP/3; cut Facebook-app tail latency 20% vs HTTP/2-over-TCP.
what_it_does: mvfst is Meta's client and server implementation of the IETF QUIC transport in C++, built on Folly (event loop, IOBuf) and Fizz (TLS 1.3). It is only the transport: applications open streams on a QuicSocket (createBidirectionalStream, writeChain, per-stream read callbacks, results returned as Expected<..., LocalErrorCode>) and run a QuicServer with one worker per event-base thread; HTTP/3 comes from Proxygen layered on top. It is not a drop-in for anything: both ends must speak QUIC, and the app sees a new stream API instead of a TCP socket.
how_it_is_fast: The measured gains are protocol-level: QUIC over UDP multiplexes streams without TCP's cross-stream head-of-line blocking, and Meta ran it with BBR as its primary congestion controller, retuning app flow-control limits and bandwidth-estimation heuristics that had been implicitly tuned for TCP. On the implementation side, the server uses a thread-local worker per core with connection IDs that encode host, worker and process IDs, so an L4 load balancer (Katran) and in-process routing avoid cross-thread handoff and survive zero-downtime restarts. Meta cut CPU cost with UDP GSO batching (also sendmmsg and sendmmsg+GSO writers), smoother userspace packet pacing, and reworked data structures for unacknowledged packets. Recent code adds an optional io_uring event-base backend, MSG_ZEROCOPY sends and an AF_XDP sender.
when_to_use: HTTP/3 or custom QUIC for mobile apps (Android/iOS) on lossy or high-latency networks where tail latency, request errors and video rebuffering matter more than bulk throughput.
You already run Folly/Fizz/Proxygen, or will adopt them, and want the QUIC stack that serves Meta's own app traffic.
Large server fleets behind an L4 load balancer: connection-ID routing that works with Katran, per-worker CPU scaling, and APIs for zero-downtime socket takeover during restarts.

Congestion-control work: Cubic, NewReno, Copa, BBR, BBR2 and static-cwnd/none ship in-tree, a Custom controller type can be plugged in, and Meta's MVFST-RL reinforcement-learning congestion-control framework targets it.
Linux servers that can use GSO/sendmmsg batching, MSG_ZEROCOPY or the optional io_uring backend to lower per-packet syscall cost.
when_not_to_use: Maximum bulk throughput per core: in the 'QUIC on the Highway' 10G benchmark (early-2023 builds), an mvfst client+server pair reached 1198 Mbit/s vs 2506 for quiche and 3004 for LSQUIC (TCP/TLS: 8010). In 2020 the maintainers cited >3 Gbps single stream on one thread and 4-5 Gbps at best on 10G, limited by kernel copies and crypto.
CPU-constrained servers: a maintainer stated (2020) that HTTP/3 over mvfst is 'not less performant than TCP + HTTP/2, albeit at a higher per-transaction CPU cost'.
Small footprint, embedded use or a C ABI: it pulls in Folly, Fizz, Boost, fmt, glog, gflags and OpenSSL, has no C API, and builds are heavy (users report getdeps filling /tmp).
Old platforms: the build includes linux/if_xdp.h, so the maintainers require Linux 4.18+ (CentOS 7 fails), and GCC 7 toolchains fail on the dependencies.
You need a stable API or semver: the README calls the API alpha, and releases are weekly date-tagged snapshots (e.g. v2026.09.21.00) that must match folly/fizz snapshots.

integration.form: static lib (CMake builds per-module static libraries, or one monolithic shared libmvfst when building shared; shared builds have had macOS link failures)
integration.dependencies: folly, fizz (TLS 1.3), Boost >=1.69 (headers), fmt, glog, gflags, OpenSSL, Threads; optional liburing (io_uring backend) and libev (alternative event base). Built most easily with Meta's getdeps.py, which fetches and builds matching versions.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (top-level CMakeLists sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20), CMake 3.14+; minimum compiler versions not documented (GCC 7 fails).
integration.platforms: Linux (4.18+ per maintainers; GSO, io_uring and AF_XDP are Linux-only), macOS and Windows (CI builds via getdeps), plus Android/iOS mobile build variants; architecture requirements not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Event-loop bound: each QuicSocket belongs to one QuicEventBase, and the headers require calls such as attach/detachEventBase from that event base's thread. The server scales with one QuicServerWorker per event-base thread, and stats callbacks are created per worker without cross-thread synchronization. There is no general thread-safety statement.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false: it replaces TCP as the transport, so both client and server must adopt it, and HTTP semantics need Proxygen's HTTP/3 layer on top.

gotchas: Defaults are not the tuned production setup: TransportSettings default to Cubic, pacingEnabled=false and batchingMode=NONE (no GSO). Maintainers say tperf defaults 'are not great' and need GSO, a large cwnd, large flow-control windows and more streams to reach Gbps rates.

The conservative default UDP send size (kDefaultV4UDPSendPacketLen = 1252 bytes) and small default flow-control windows (65 KiB per stream, 1 MiB per connection) cap throughput on high-bandwidth-delay links. One user got ~290 Mbit/s on a 500 Mbit/s emulated link until raising the receive window (#166).

Security history: CVE-2021-24029 (a crafted packet causes a crash via a failed assertion, CVSS 7.5) and CVE-2025-30403 (heap-buffer-overflow, CVSS 8.1, fixed in v2025.07.07.00). Until a 2026 fix, replayed packets were decrypted and processed again (#428). Track the weekly tags.
Performance depends on the peer: in the 10G study the mvfst-client/picoquic-server pair got only 52 Mbit/s, and over emulated GEO satellite links mvfst did well as a server but poorly as a client.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick mvfst over LSQUIC, ngtcp2, picoquic, TQUIC or quiche when you are on Meta's Folly/Fizz/Proxygen stack or need its fleet features (Katran-aware connection-ID routing, socket takeover, pluggable BBR/Copa); pick LSQUIC or ngtcp2 when goodput per core or a small C library matters. Like Google QUICHE's entry, its evidence is a production A/B against the operator's own TCP stack, not a cross-stack benchmark.
verified_claims_summary: Meta's staged production rollout of QUIC/HTTP-3 (mvfst + Proxygen, BBR as primary congestion control) in the Facebook app, against its prior HTTP/2-over-TCP stack, reported 20% lower tail latency (percentile unstated), 6% fewer request errors and 5% smaller response headers on dynamic requests, plus up to 22% better mean time between rebuffering, 8% fewer errors and 20% fewer stalls on video. No hardware, compiler, network mix or fixed workload is given, and app flow-control and bandwidth heuristics were retuned, so this measures the protocol switch, not mvfst's code speed.
status_note: Actively developed by Meta (last push 2026-09-26, weekly date-tagged snapshots up to v2026.09.21.00) and MIT-licensed, but the README still calls the API alpha, and in practice it builds only with matching Folly/Fizz versions via getdeps.
